about.title: Slope and Rate of Change
about.length_note: About 30 minutes. This class covers one main idea (slope) in four forms: a graph, two points, a table and a real-world rate. Each idea has a short check question, so it fits a half-hour class. If it feels rushed, stop after beat 12 and do the table and rate-of-change beats next time.

say.text: Welcome to class 13. Today we learn one number that describes a whole straight line: its slope.

show.text: Slope and Rate of Change

say.text: Think of a ramp. Some ramps are gentle and some are steep. Slope is the math word for that tilt.

show.text: Two skate ramps side by side. The left ramp is gentle and the right ramp is steep. Both climb from left to right.

say.text: To measure the tilt, we use two moves. Rise is how far you go up or down. Run is how far you go across.

show.text: Rise = vertical change (up or down) | Run = horizontal change (left or right)

say.text: Slope is the rise compared with the run. We write it as m equals rise over run.

show.text: slope: m = rise / run

say.text: Here is a line through (1, 2) and (4, 8). Draw a right triangle between the points. Count the rise: 2 up to 8 is 6. Count the run: 1 across to 4 is 3.

show.text: A coordinate grid with a line through (1, 2) and (4, 8). A right triangle sits under it. The vertical side is labeled 6 and the horizontal side is labeled 3.

say.text: Now divide: 6 over 3 is 2. The slope is 2. That means up 2 for every 1 across.
Your turn. A line goes up 6 while it goes across 4. What is its slope?

show.text: rise 6, run 4

ask.q: A line rises 6 and runs 4. What is its slope?
ask.why: Slope is rise over run, so the rise 6 goes on top and the run 4 goes on the bottom. Flipping them gives 2/3, which is a different tilt.

say.text: Signs matter. Up is a positive rise and down is a negative rise. Right is a positive run and left is a negative run.

show.text: Rise: up = positive, down = negative | Run: right = positive, left = negative

say.text: Read the line from left to right, like a book. If it climbs, the slope is positive. If it falls, the slope is negative. Example: down 3 while going right 2 gives rise -3 over run 2, so the slope is -3/2.

show.text: Two lines on a grid. One climbs left to right and is labeled positive. One falls left to right and is labeled negative. A small triangle on the falling line shows rise -3 and run 2.

ask.q: You read a line from left to right and it goes downhill. Is its slope positive or negative?
ask.why: A line that falls from left to right has a negative rise for a positive run, so the slope is negative.

say.text: What if the line is flat? Then you never go up or down. The rise is 0, so the slope is 0. Take y = 4: rise 0, run 3, and 0 over 3 is 0.

show.text: Horizontal line y = b has slope 0

ask.q: What is the slope of the line y = -5?
ask.why: y = -5 is a horizontal line. Every horizontal line has slope 0 because the rise is 0.

say.text: Now a straight-up wall. A vertical line has run 0, so we would be dividing by zero. We can't do that, so we say the slope is undefined.

show.text: Vertical line x = a has undefined slope

ask.q: What is the slope of the line x = 8?
ask.why: x = 8 is a vertical line, so the run is 0. Dividing by 0 is not allowed, so the slope is undefined. A slope of 0 belongs to flat, horizontal lines.

say.text: A memory trick: zero slope is flat, like a floor. Undefined slope is straight up, like a wall.

show.text: Zero slope = horizontal (floor) | Undefined slope = vertical (wall)

say.text: Sometimes there is no graph, only two points. Then use the slope formula: change in y over change in x.
Try (2, 7) and (6, 1). Rise: 1 minus 7 is -6. Run: 6 minus 2 is 4. So the slope is -6/4, or -3/2. Keep the same point first on the top and the bottom.
Your turn with the formula. Use the points (1, 2) and (3, 8).

ask.q: What is the slope of the line through (1, 2) and (3, 8)?
ask.why: The rise is 8 - 2 = 6 and the run is 3 - 1 = 2. So the slope is 6/2 = 3.

say.text: Tables work the same way. Each row is a point. In this game, x is minutes played and y is coins earned.
Pick two rows, (0, 10) and (2, 40). The rise is 30 coins and the run is 2 minutes. 30 over 2 is 15.
Does it matter which two rows we pick? For a straight line, no. The rate is the same between any two points.

show.text: A line has the same slope everywhere

ask.q: Use the rows (2, 40) and (6, 100) from the table. What is the slope?
ask.why: The rise is 100 - 40 = 60 and the run is 6 - 2 = 4. So 60/4 = 15, the same as before. A line has the same slope between any two points.

say.text: That 15 is a rate of change. It tells how much y changes for each 1 step in x. Here it is 15 coins per minute.

show.text: 15 coins per minute

say.text: A rate compares two different units, like coins and minutes. So say the units when you say the slope: y-units per x-unit.

show.text: Slope with units = rate of change

say.text: Try it with money. A job pays $30 for 2 hours and $90 for 5 hours. Find the slope and say what it means.

show.text: 2 hours -> $30 | 5 hours -> $90

ask.q: 2 hours pays $30 and 5 hours pays $90. What does the slope tell you?
ask.right: $20 per hour: each extra hour adds $20
ask.why: The rise is 90 - 30 = 60 dollars and the run is 5 - 2 = 3 hours. 60/3 = 20, so the pay rises $20 for each hour.

say.text: One preview. A straight line has one constant rate. A curve has a rate that changes, so later we find an average rate of change between two points.

show.text: Line: constant rate of change | Curve: rate of change varies

say.text: Let's put it together. Slope is rise over run. From a graph you count it. From two points or a table you subtract. In a story it is a rate with units.

show.text: Graph: count rise and run | Two points: (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1) | Table: pick two rows | Horizontal: 0 | Vertical: undefined

ask.q: A line goes through (0, 4) and (2, 0). What is its slope?
ask.why: The rise is 0 - 4 = -4 and the run is 2 - 0 = 2. So -4/2 = -2. The line falls from left to right, so a negative slope makes sense.

other_side.claim: The slope of a vertical line is called undefined, not zero.
other_side.other_view: Some sources say a vertical line's slope can be treated as infinite, since the run is 0. Other sources say infinity is not a real number, so in algebra courses the right answer is simply undefined. In this course we use undefined.
